speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: EXTENSION, FROM APRIL 30 TO MAY 31, OF DATE OF FILING CERTAIN RETURNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to make a statement with reference to the filing of income tax returns for the year 1947.
Extreme weather conditions in various parts of the country are making it impossible for taxpayers to get the appropriate income tax forms. In addition, there is a substantial increase, particularly in rural areas, in the number of taxpayers over the previous year. This has added greatly to the problem of distributing the various forms.
For these and other reasons, many taxpayers throughout the country are finding it extremely difficult to complete and file their returns on time.
As a consequence, the government has decided that the time for filing 1947 individual income tax returns will be extended from April 30 to May 31, 1948. This applies only to those returns known as T.l General, T.l Special, T.4-T.1 employees, T.l Farmers and T.l Prairie Farmers.
The penalty for late filing will be assessed if the taxpayer fails to file his return on or before May 31, 1948.
Individual taxpayers who ordinarily would be required to pay the balance of their tax on or before April 30, 1948, must now make payment of that balance on or before May 31, 1948. If they fail to do so, interest will be charged from that date.
72-1948-1 i
This extension does not relieve those taxpayers who are required to make quarterly or other instalment payments, from making such payments when due, nor does it relieve them from interest on any arrears of such instalments.
All returns, other than those listed above, required to be filed under the statute, must be filed on the due date.

speechtext:
In that regard I take seoond place, however, only to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
In rising to say a word on the motion for third reading of Bill No. 203, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, I do so because of certain statements which have been made from time to time with respect to this party's position on unemployment insurance. It is necessary, although I am sorry that it becomes so, for us again to place our record so clearly on the record that even those who are desirous of altering that record will not be able to do so without bringing upon themselves the condemnation of the electorate.
I have a personal reason for rising at this time, sir, because down through the years as a member of parliament, along with others in the Progressive Conservative party, I have taken a consistent and, I think, a vigorous stand in seeking legislation by this government with respect to unemployment insurance. It must be remembered that the party now in power had unemployment insurance in its platform as far back as the year 1919. It must be remembered also, Mr. Speaker, for those whose memory at times becomes conveniently forgetful, that it was not the Liberal party or the C.C.F. party, but rather the Conservative party, which in 1935 had the honour of bringing in the first bill for unemployment insurance in Canada. In addition to that-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRIBUTIONS, PROCEDURE, OFFENCES AND PENALTIES
speechtext: The Conservatives did not bring in unemployment insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRIBUTIONS, PROCEDURE, OFFENCES AND PENALTIES
speechtext:
We shall let the hon. member make his speech again, although I doubt if it is necessary. Not only was it our party that brought unemployment insurance legislation for the first time into the House of Commons, but it was this party as well which, during the sessions of 1936 and following years, saw the present government sending legislation which had been passed in the House of Commons to the Supreme Court of Canada and elsewhere for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not it was constitutional. This had the result of delaying legisla-lation from 1936 until 1940, when it was finally passed.
In 1940 the present government brought in a new measure with respect to unemployment insurance. I was one of those who tried to take a little lead, so far as our own party was concerned, in promoting and attempting to improve the measure that had been brought

down. I was a member of the special committee on unemployment insurance which was set up under the chairmanship of the then minister of labour, Mr. McLarty, and had much to do with the various debates and discussions which finally resulted in an unemployment insurance measure being passed by the House of Commons. That was in the year 1940. It was in that year that the measure received its third reading.
The point I wish to make is this. Nowhere in this report of the special committee on unemployment insurance which I hold in my hand will anyone find the slightest suggestion of any opposition on the part of the Conservative party to unemployment insurance or its principles, and scarcely any to its details. In addition, if one turns to Hansard of July 19, 1940, one finds that the Minister of Labour himself put his imprimatur on the position of our party at that time. This was toward the end of the debate, when the legislation was finally going through. At page 1786 of Hansard for 1940 Mr. McLarty said, with a great deal of truth:
It has been a congenial task for me as minister, sponsoring a bill such as this, to have received such wholehearted approval of the measure, in principle, as has been given this bill.
In addition, I was looking up the records and found that going back from third reading, which is indicated at page 2088 of Hansard for that session, at every single stage the bill went through without division and without amendment, and with the wholehearted approval of the Conservative party of that day.
That makes it very difficult for me, after such an active part in the consideration of that legislation as I tried to take at that time, to swallow the remark made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) over the air last Thursday night. This is what the minister said in that broadcast on The Nation's Business:
Next, look at unemployment insurance, introduced by the Liberals in 1941

Well, he was so much asleep that he even missed the year the measure was introduced. -and opposed by the Conservatives; another measure of social security introduced and put into effect by the Liberals.
I resent that statement, which was made over the air more than a week ago. The minister has had plenty of time since to correct it. If he did not know that was not the fact, he should have known it. If he did know it was not the fact, then I think this house and this party deserve an apology from the minister for having made that statement.

Unemployment Insurance Act
I well remember my old schoolmaster in the town of Brampton giving this good advice to his students: "You cannot at the same time whistle and chew a meal, and do justice to both". Neither can the Minister of National Defence look after our armed forces and at the same time keep an eye upon his political fences, as he was trying to do in that broadcast the other evening.
I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the minister that what we need is a man with both eyes on the defence of Canada. I want to say also that instead of taking his little pencil and trying to figure out the total time that has been taken up by some members of parliament, and what we have been saying in Hansard, he had better get out a great big pencil and figme the total strength of the armed forces of this country, for I can tell him those are the totals in which the people of this country are interested, not in all this small political nonsense that has gone over the air under the title The Nation's Business.
I would not have risen at all had I not keenly resented the suggestion that I and others who tried to do a good job in the committee which considered that measure, had opposed this legislation. I resent it when someone who should know better comes along and makes that statement. The minister was here then; but if he was asleep at that time I hope he will not continue to sleep now that he has such a big job as the defence of Canada. So far as our position is concerned, I hope it will be made clear in this instance as it should have been made clear in the instance brought up by the minister. Our name should be cleared of a blot and stain which it is beneath the dignity of any member of the government to attempt to put upon us.

The house resumed from Monday, April 26, consideration in committee of Bill No. 211, to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Member of the force; member.

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel this may be the only opportunity I shall have to say a word in commendation of the splendid service rendered by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I believe they are appreciated by the people of Canada as an outstanding force in the regulation of law and order.
I was pleased to note that in the advertising prepared by the Ontario government for tourist purposes a full page was devoted to the work of the mounted police; and at a conference held in Toronto the only persons who found fault with that advertising were the two communist members of the provincial legislature.
I feel that those who are seeking to visit our country are impressed by the fact that this is a country in which law and order is respected. We as citizens of Canada appreciate more and more the service rendered by this great force. Indeed the regulations under which they work impose upon them great sacrifices which, for the glory of their unit, they are prepared to make. Throughout the length and breadth of the universe the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is known as the force that always gets its man.
During the past few summers, tourist vessels from Chicago and other points in the United States have been calling at my home city of Owen Sound. This splendid unit, the mounted police, have always provided an officer dressed in his scarlet uniform at that port. Let me say that citizens of the United States respect this police force, just as Canadians do. They feel that when they set foot on Canadian soil they are entering a land where freedom and justice prevail and where law and order is maintained.
I have taken this opportunity to pay my compliments and tribute to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
A number of questions were asked the other night about administration in general, and in particular as to the matter of investigation of subversive elements in the country. In concluding the debate the minister said that those matters did not arise particularly at this time and could not very well be answered or discussed by him. I do feel however that the country as a whole would like to have a general statement from the minister at this time with respect to the work being done. No other opportunity will arise for discussion of this matter. It is one that is being given much attention in the press of Canada, and of the United States as well. I refer to the whole matter of investigations made by the police forces having to do with subversive activities connected with communism.
I mentioned the other evening one matter which affects thousands of people in the prairie provinces, namely, the subtle forms of intimidation that are being practised by certain individuals in this country in order to extract from the people assistance for communist endeavours in other parts of the world.
I am not asking anything out of the way when I ask for a statement in this connection; for Mr. Hoover, the head of the federal bureau of investigation in the United States, has set forth in detail what that organization is doing. His statements, made in general terms, have given the people of the United States some idea of the extent to which subversive elements are widespread throughout that country, and also the measures being taken to prevent their continuance or development.
The other day I raised the question of intimidation of racial groups. I know that the minister within the last few days has received certain suggestions and recommendations in that regard. Representatives of an anti-communist group, persons of Slavic origin, came here and placed the matter before him. They were asking for some assurance that they would be protected against this sort of thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext: Against what?

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
Against the threats that were being held out that harm would be done to their relatives in continental Europe unless they adopted the suggestions of those who had got in touch with them. These men who were here the other day said that they had called a meeting in Toronto with a view to building up a solid front against communist activities. A number of persons with whom they had communicated said frankly to them that they were fearful
of attending any meeting, of showing their hand in any way, or of contributing their efforts to the combating of communist activities. These operators had instilled in their hearts the fear that should they act or show their hands their relatives abroad would be endangered.
After all, this is a matter under the jurisdiction of the minister, and I should like to know what the department is doing in this regard. Does it contemplate the introduction of an amendment to widen the sections of the criminal code which cannot now be used to punish those who do this kind of thing? If the legislation is widened it is possible that the relatives might be proceeded against, but in any event the fact that such legislation was on the statute book would in itself be a deterrent.
I should like to have a statement from the minister with regard to a number of matters affecting mounted police administration in respect to which the members of the force would like to have certain changes made. I shall not repeat them, because repetition will not make them any clearer. Would the minister be willing to indicate to the committee the attitude of the department toward these questions, and whether or not any changes are contemplated other than those covered by the bill which has been introduced?
I believe that when this force, which is great in service and magnificent in tradition, asks for the removal of a number of little pinpricking things, every consideration should be given to their request. The amendments provided for by this bill go a long way toward removing serious complaint. Over a period of two or three years we on this side of the house asked for an increase in the salaries of the mounted police, but the answer was that they were getting reasonably good pay. We pointed to the number of fully qualified men who had served only five years but who resigned or retired because of the hopelessness of their position as they saw it. I understand that normally a man must be in the service eleven years before he achieves the highest salary paid to a constable. Promotions have been too slow and opportunities for advancement too restricted. These things which they object to should be remedied if possible.
I come now to one other matter, the personnel report. I was joined in this by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe). The fact that the constable may not express his views in connection with adverse personnel reports affecting him has caused a great deal of resentment. We are asking the members of the R.C.M.P. to discharge great

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act
responsibilities. Our safety depends on them. I suggest that we in this house should do everything we can to remove anything that might cause them not to have that degree of contentment without which efficient work is impossible.
I want the minister to understand that we are not in the position in which the minister of defence endeavoured to put us the other day. We are here to place suggestions before the government. We want to co-operate in this matter. The people are asking, through us, for the assurance of the Minister of Justice that all is well so far as internecine activities which might undermine the country are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, naturally I came in with the thought that the bill would be taken up section by section, but I shall answer the questions asked by the hon. gentleman in so far as I can.
I am not in a position to make a statement about the program of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in watching communists in Canada. I do not think it would be desirable for me to make such a statement in the house, ft is well known that for many years the R.C.M.P. has been keenly alive to the possibilities of subversive action, and I think they are as much alive today as they ever were, perhaps more so. If it is possible to make a more comprehensive statement without defeating the end that is sought, I will see if one can bs prepared and delivered on another occasion. I submit that the proper occasion for that would be on the estimates of the mounted police rather than on this bill.
With regard to the other questions that were asked, I should like to deal with one to which a number of speakers gave some attention the other night. I refer to the question of threats to persons of foreign origin or foreign parentage. Apart from those that were made across the floor of the house the other night, the only representation that has ever been made in this regard was contained in a letter which I received from a solicitor in western Canada advising me that a client or a person who had consulted him had stated that injury had been threatened to his relatives in one of the communist countries of Europe if he did not do certain things. I forget whether he was to join a communist organization, contribute to a communist organization or what it was. However, that is irrelevant.
This solicitor suggested that there should be an amendment to the criminal code to go beyond the present section dealing with threats to parents and other relatives. I

turned that over to officers of the Department of Justice and asked them to advise me whether such an amendment could be drafted and whether in their opinion it was desirable. Since the speeches were made the other night, in which several hon. members said that officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police themselves said that this is becoming almost a practice throughout the country, and after consulting an hon. member or two on this side of the house who said that there was some talk about it, I tried to ascertain just what, if anything, is going on. The information I got is that occasionally in conversation there is some reference to relatives of the displaced person or other person of foreign origin or foreign parentage in the home country or communist country. These references are not threats; they are merely reminders, I suppose, or hints rather than threats.

speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY

In a minute, yes. I have asked the deputy minister of justice to see whether any strengthening of the criminal code is possible in that regard, and he advised me at noon that he would work on it this afternoon. I do not think the house should have too high hopes of anything of much value being done, because certainly it seems to me that if I were a communist approaching a non-communist with a view to getting him to contribute money or do something else of that kind, I would not be making a threat. It is a little difficult for me to understand how a reference to his family in the old country could be made the subject of a criminal prosecution. I think it would be pretty difficult; but as I say, the Department of Justice is giving consideration to something of that kind.
Whether it would accomplish anything, even if proper criminal legislation could be passed, is another question; because I doubt whether any information would ever be given. If we did have legislation of that kind I doubt whether anyone would1 ever inform or lay a charge. Certainly he would not if he had any real fear of retaliation or prosecution of his relatives in the country from which he came.
My hon. friend asked whether any other amendment to the act was proposed at this session. The answer is no. These are the amendments that were proposed for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act at the present session. I think that they deal with everything that needs to be dealt with. They do not deal with everything that has been

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act
brought before the department for attention; they do not by any means adopt all the suggestions that have been made, but I think they include all the suggestions that should be acted upon.
May I say a word with regard to pay. My hon. friend said that for years it has been urged that the pay of the R.C.M.P. has not been high enough. Well, the pay that is adequate today may not be adequate tomorrow. I have no reason to think that the pay of this force has not been comparable with that of other forces and with the armed services throughout the years. Recently, of course, there have been increases to the civil service and to the armed forces, and the time had come when another pay increase was desirable for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; that pay increase has been provided for by regulation. I think the force is fairly well satisfied with the pay increases that have been provided.
A question has been raised about the rule that members of the force are not shown reports on themselves.	The commissioner

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext: It is a complicated matter. The hon. gentleman is now taking the case of a superannuated member of the force who for some reason is making contributions to the dependent's pension fund.

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext: I think I am correct in this; this is my information. If the person is superannuated he would not be making contributions to that fund unless he were paying up for back service of some kind. He has an option under this bill of changing to the new pension scheme contemplated in this bill. Any person now in the force may change over from the present pension plan to the new pension plan, and provisions for transition are provided for. If he wishes to remain with the present pension plan he has the option of doing so. I presume hon. members understand the difference in principle between the two pension plans. The present pension plan provides for a free pension to the member, but a wholly member-financed pension for the dependents. The government makes no contribution to the dependent's pension under the present system, but the member of the force makes no contribution to his own pension. Every present member of the force who wishes to continue along that line may do so. Of course none of his contractual rights are taken away from him.

speechtext:
I asked the minister some questions the other night about the superannuation scheme. When the new scheme is inaugurated I hope it will be a scheme where-
3414	COMMONS
Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act_
by, when a man decides to take advantage of the superannuation act, he will not have to continue to make payments after he has paid to the government everything he owes them. I tried to explain to the house the situation with regard to the wardens in our penitentiaries who come under a scheme such as this. They had so much to pay because they had not already made those payments, but after they had paid that up and were all clear they still had to keep on making payments until the day they died. That is not a good scheme, and I raise my voice against it now. I would ask the government not to have a scheme like that but to see to it that when a man has paid his dues to the government he will not be required to keep on paying until he dies, because there are some people who live to ninety.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME- COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must be under some misapprehension. This is quite simple-at least if I can make it so. The principle that applies to penitentiary employees is exactly the same as the principle that applies in the civil service. A man may have temporary service when there is no deduction from his pay, and that arrangement may go on for ten years. He may then become permanent and may wish to take advantage of the superannuation fund. He may desire to have the time during which he was not making contributions count for pension purposes. If he wishes to have that time count for pension purposes he must make the contribution in respect of that period. He must pay 5, 5J or 6 per cent, as the case may be, of the pay he received during that period in which he made no contributions, and he must pay interest on it, into the superannuation fund. If he pays that in a lump sum, that is the end and he needs to make no further contributions. But many persons are not in a position to make a lump-sum payment. Many persons desire to have deductions made in the future, either from pay or sometimes from pension, until they die, and a calculation is made to determine how much shall be deducted from pension to be put into the fund, being that amount which the person had not contributed in respect of the period during which he was not under the superannuation provision, when he was merely a temporary. That is the reason these deductions continue until death. There is one suggestion I wish to make with regard to the question of intimidation. The intimidation is undoubtedly very real; it does exist. The minister asked how the criminal code might be amended. I suggest to him that any organization or any individual collecting funds for use outside Canada, for charitable purposes or for a service outside Canada, should be registered with the federal government. During the war we had the War Charities Act and it created no great hardship in the raising of funds for charities. Much of the intimidation comes from persons who have been citizens ofj or who are descended from persons who were citizens of countries behind what is known as the iron curtain. They approach others asking for donations for charitable or other purposes. A great deal of the trouble in this respect might be overcome if the appropriate act, whether it be the criminal code or some other statute, were amended to provide that anyone soliciting funds for charitable purposes or for other uses outside Canada should be registered with the federal government. I believe that is in accordance with what the United States government has done, and it is particularly useful in this country, where we have had recently a number of serious attempts at intimidation, particularly of displaced persons. Persons coming to this country, often with little or no knowledge of our language, have frequently been met and have been made to undergo certain pressure tactics by communist groups to join the communist party. In any case their faith in the democratic system under which we live in Canada is exposed to danger and may be shaken. I think that has been proved in numbers of cases, and is particularly true of displaced persons coming from Europe to work in the mining and logging industries.
There is one more case which received a good deal of attention in the press recently. That is the case of the Soviet embassy's advertising in the foreign language newspapers of this country, particularly the Baltic language newspapers, and stating that it was necessary for those persons who were Baltic citizens at one time to register with the Soviet embassy. I believe that case has been taken up by the Department of External Affairs.
Nevertheless, that advertisement constituted a definite threat to those people who read the foreign language newspapers and whose knowledge of English is not great or is perhaps nonexistent. In my opinion that amounts to a threat. Not only that, it amounts to an abuse by the Soviet embassy of its rights and is a departure from the ordinary course of diplomatic behaviour in Canada or in any other country. No Canadian embassy would ever dream of doing such a thing in any foreign country, and I consider this definitely amounts to a threat. That case is particularly interesting today when, although perhaps from a de jure point of view there is a difference between the Soviet government and the communist party, there is perhaps no difference from a de facto point of view. I believe the government should consider an amendment to the criminal code particularly with regard to that matter.
I have one more suggestion to make with regard to pay to the mounted police. In the force today there are a number of officers who must undertake special extra training. I am thinking of the matter from the technical point of view, and am referring to those who are doing, shall we say, flying operations or special operations with regard to medical and legal work. These men must have high technical qualifications. Frequently they are university graduates. I believe that some recognition of these extra duties should be given in this act. I have read the act cursorily, but I believe that the men who are thus specially trained should receive special consideration with regard to pay.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is with regard to these men who are doing work in the intelligence department of this great force. An intelligence officer frequently does not wear a uniform. He must assume various types of dress. He is required to mingle in all classes of society. In this day and age he must be a diplomatic and cosmopolitan person indeed. Particularly with regard to the clothing and travelling allowances of persons doing this work, I think the regulations should be made more liberal so that under no circumstances will an officer of the force who is doing intelligence work ever need to think of the extra cost of, shall we say, spoiling his civilian clothes or having to take, in the line of duty, chances which might damage his property. I mention that matter inasmuch as several officers have mentioned it to me.

I will go a step farther. There is a definite circulation of subversive literature going on in certain parts of the country. I am wondering if steps are being taken to stamp this type of thing out. I should like to cite to the minister one instance which occurred quite recently. Within the last two or three weeks a man was caught distributing, in the dead of night, this particular subversive literature. He was brought in by one of the local police officers. He was caught with a copy of the literature. He openly defied the police officer and said, "I am a communist and proud of it." That was his attitude, and these threats are actually being made.
There has come to my attention something else, which perhaps the minister knows about; that is, the practice of sending teen-age children back to certain foreign countries, supposedly for education. Several people of European origin have told me of being approached in this connection, and that many of these children have gone back. I believe the country concerned, as far as I was told, was Czechoslovakia. I should like to know if there is any law or regulation under which
Canadian citizenship could be taken away from any person proved guilty of doing things of this kind. I think that would have a definite effect, because they value that citizenship and guard it closely once they get it, since it protects them in case they get in trouble and go a step too far.
I mention these things so that the minister may know the anxiety I feel, because I have come closely in touch with these matters; and I have other information I want to pass on to the officers of the mounted police within a very few days. I am digging up more all the time.

An N.C.O. on detachment may conscientiously carry out such orders or instructions, but somewhere someone may err. The commissioned officer is in a position to lay a charge against the N.C.O. He may also hear the charge, and may also impose sentence, though the original error in judgment, made in good faith, may be attributable to the commissioned officer involved. It seems to me the N.C.O. is placed in a most unfortunate position. He is not represented by counsel. It is not as though the charge is being heard in a civil court. I am not going to take very much time, Mr. Chairman, nor shall I go over the ground already covered with respect to this fine body of men. On more than one occasion I have gone on record in that regard. I remember that in the Nova Scotia legislature in 1929 I said I felt that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be a much better body of men to carry out the work of patrolling our province than men selected locally, 5849-2171
because they would be a more independent body, and for other reasons I mentioned at that time. So I do not propose to deal with that point at all beyond saying that I believe the Halifax division is composed of men of a very fine type. I believe I should make that statement because of the splendid type of service they have given, not only in the capital city but throughout the province.
I wish to bring two matters to the attention of the minister, because I consider them important in view of the effect they may have on the service. I notice that in section 1 it is proposed to drop the word "marine." Unless I hear very good reasons for it, I am inclined to think this is a mistake. In the Department of National Defence we have the armj-, navy and air force, each with its own work to do, but all under one head and operating efficiently. I believe it is a good thing to have them all under one department. But I say that on the east and west coasts the marine section has a certain type of work, and does that work well. Instead of dropping the marine section, I would hope there would be a general expansion of the branch, and added duties which would perhaps give us greater protection along the shore and at the same time carry out a still greater degree of rescue work.
I feel that if the marine section of the mounted police were expanded or enlarged it could be closely co-operative with the Royal Canadian Air Force, and perform the duties carried on by the coast guard in the United States. They could be of valuable assistance along the Atlantic shoreline, and I suggest that the minister might discuss this matter with the commissioner who, I believe, appreciates the points I am raising. What I have said about the Atlantic coast applies equally to the west coast. That is all I wish to say about the marine section. I thought it was a mistake to drop the word "marine". It is about the same as taking away the uniform worn by members of the mounted .police.
There are two other matters I would bring to the attention of the minister. The first has to do with the transfer of men from one section of the country to another. This is done often. Perhaps it is a matter which the commissioner and officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police understand more fully than I do. However, with t.he housing situation as it is throughout certain sections of Canada, and in view of the fact that a number of these men are married, it seems to me unreasonable and not in the best interests of those concerned to transfer a man from Halifax to

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act
Vancouver, or from Halifax to Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto, where housing conditions are similar to those we have in Halifax. A man for a long period of time would have to maintain two homes. I should think that at the present time it would be good policy not to bring about any unnecessary transfers; indeed it would be wise to keep them at the lowest possible minimum.
Then, it is my understanding that transportation is provided upon a man's leaving the force or retiring therefrom. The rule is that a man taking his superannuation must signify immediately his intention of moving to a certain section of the country. A short time ago a member of the force took his superannuation; but when, in the regular way, he was asked the question as to whether he wanted transportation he was unable to say that he did require it. He had been unable to secure housing accommodation where he wished to go, and for that reason was unable to accept transportation, or to say, "Yes; I want transportation for my wife, myself and furniture". Two months later he did find a house and then made application for transportation, this time only for himself and his wife, without the furniture. I feel that there should be a time limit, or that some leeway should be given, so that cases of this kind could be given favourable consideration. I quite realize that regulations must be followed; but common sense should be exercised and a certain degree of reasonableness shown in borderline cases like this one.
I have presented these facts as briefly as I could, sincerely hoping that, with his usual good judgment, the minister will give them the attention they deserve.

Before I take my seat there is one more question I should like to ask the minister. Does the R.C.M.P. carry out secret service work, or is there a secret service or intelligence

branch in Canada? Perhaps I had better put it this way. There is such a thing as military service. Is that a separate branch from the R.C.M.P., or is there such a branch? Is the R.C.M.P. the branch of government service that takes care of intelligence work throughout the country? If that is so, then their work becomes highly specialized.
I am interested in this for more reasons than one, which I think can readily be guessed. There are more dangers in this country than most of us realize. When we think of espionage and sabotage we think in terms of blowing up a public building, a factory, a ship or something like that, but there are more than buildings and factories that can be sabotaged. The thinking and the minds of the Canadian people can be sabotaged. That is a branch of intelligence which seldom comes into the picture, but it is an important one, because what is happening today in Canada and what has happened in the past is conditioning our own people to receive that which is absolutely foreign to our concept of democratic citizenship.

My chief purpose in rising now is to ask the minister a question. I refer to a particular case and the decision made in that case, namely, an officer or constable of the R.C.M.P. who served the forces well and

faithfully for many years prior to the war. He asked for his release from the R.C.M.P. in order to become a D.A.P.M. with the R.C.A.F. He was released from the service of the R.C.M.P. in order to join the R.C.A.F. He was one of the first of the D.A.P.M's. I personally saw him at work, and for the time that he was with me he did a perfectly magnificent job of a highly specialized nature. He continued to do his good work; he was promoted consistently until he attained the rank of wing commander, which was a very high rank, as the minister knows, for a D.A.P.M. During the course of his duty he had to report to Newfoundland, and during a trip there he was torpedoed and suffered a severe illness consequent upon the exposure. However, he ultimately returned to duty where he remained until the end of the war, and then he endeavoured to rejoin the R.C.M.P. At that time he was told he was over-age and could no longer be a constable in the R.C.M.P. He had retired from the R.C.A.F. because his services were no longer required. He had been released from the R.C.M.P. and could not rejoin them because he was over-age. He now finds himself with only a very small pension from the R.C.A.F. and with no pension whatsoever from the R.C.M.P. and no hope of getting any.
It would seem to me that the position of that man is most incongruous. He did not leave the R.C.M.P. to take up some civilian employment or to get a better job or really to change his duties. He virtually changed his uniform. The service in the R.C.M.P. is the service of his country; the service in the R.C.A.F. is the service of his country. Just because he wears a different uniform for six years he loses the benefits of a pension, and that man today, living in British Columbia as he does, is endeavouring to eke out an existence and not too successfully. It appears on the surface that if what has been done is within the four corners of the act in regard to pension, then the act is definitely at fault.

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Northwest Territories Act.
He said: I do not want to delay the passing of this simple bill, Mr. Speaker, but I think I should make a brief statement. Supplementing the information given in the explanatory notes, I may say that even before the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces in 1930 the provincial governments administered the game and fur regulations. Similarly, the Yukon territorial government deals with these matters by territorial ordinances. It is desired to place the Northwest Territories council in exactly the same position so that the .administration of these particular resources which are of such intimate concern to the local people should be subject to control and administration by the Northwest Territories council. This will enable necessary changes in policy to be made effective promptly to meet the changes which
Northwest Territories Act

often occur suddenly owing to climatic conditions or forest fires. Already the Northwest Territories council has been authorized to fix and does fix the royalties which must be paid by those exporting fur from the territories.
The other feature of this legislation is the provision which will enable appeals from the judgment of stipendiary magistrates in civil matters. In criminal matters there is already a right to appeal to a provincial court, as set out in the criminal code. The reason why this amendment only provides the right to appeal to the Alberta courts is that the only stipendiary magistrates are in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories, which is directly north of Alberta.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Appellate jurisdiction from stipendiary magistrate.

subtopic: PRESERVATION OF GAME-APPELLATE JURISDICTION FROM STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATE
speechtext:
I wish simply to point out to the minister who is in charge of the bill and to the committee that the wording of the section which provides that appeal from stipendiary magistrates in the Northwest Territories, which territories include the district of Mackenzie, is to the appellate division of the supreme court of Alberta, which is quite appropriate. This emphasizes what I have repeatedly pointed out to the minister, to the government and to the house, namely the impropriety of having added the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories to Yukon as an electoral district. Appeals from all parts of Yukon go, not to the appellate court of Alberta but to the appellate court of British Columbia, because in fact practically all the business and all the communications of the Northwest Territories go to British Columbia on the west coast of Canada.
At this session of parliament I hope the minister and his government will see their way clear to undo the wrong that has been done to the people of the Mackenzie district and of the Yukon in uniting them as an electoral district. Because of the importance of the Mackenzie district, I believe the people of Mackenzie are entitled to a member in this house, just as the territory of Yukon has had a member for many years. It has never had a population which would entitle it to a member, but because of its importance as a producer of wealth in this dominion it has been given that privilege. The Mackenzie district is in exactly the same position, and the govem-

ment should follow the same course in connection with Mackenzie that has been followed in connection with Yukon.

As one coming from another part of Canada than that w'hich the hon. member who has just spoken comes from, I wish to add a word in support of what he has said with respect to the joining of these two very large areas in one electoral district. This is a matter which normally would arise in another debate, but I hope the chairman and the committee wdll bear with me, because I am not going to take much time now.
It seems to me that the situation in Yukon has been accepted and recognized for many years, and as far as I know there has never been any desire on the part of residents of the Yukon to make any change There we have a small population, but there are special problems in the Yukon which I think call for a member of parliament who is particularly conversant with the situation there. We in central Canada have no conception of the problems that arise, as a result of the distances which must be covered in that constituency, in connection with electoral representation in the House of Commons.
So it is in the case of Mackenzie, which seems likely to become an important and more thickly populated part of this country. It seems to me that they need a member of their own to assist in the development of that district. The situation in connection with representation there is far different from the situation with respect to other great sections of our population which perhaps have a greater past than future, though this may not apply to many districts in Canada. Nevertheless it seems to me that legislation of this kind, and similar matters which may arise from time to time in future, urgently demand the presence in this house of a member representing that district, in order to guide, promote and advance the development that is sure to take place in the Northwest Territories.
It is really a scandal that this house should have added the Northwest Territories to Yukon, when each district has special problems which are difficult enough to handle as it is, without trying to throw the problems of both districts into the lap of one man. I appreciate the privilege you have given me, Mr. Chairman, of saying these few words. I know my remarks have been out of order, but I do not apologize for having made them because I believe this matter goes to the very root of the development of the Northwest Territories. We believe that Yukon is entitled to a member, and certainly the Mackenzie district is equally entitled to a member. It seems to me

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF UNDERTAKINGS UPON LANDS OF THE DOMINION

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 11, to amend the Dominion Water Power Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think I should make a brief statement at this time. Early in 1946 it was decided to expedite the economic development of the Northwest Territories, including the expansion of the mining industry, by the development of a hydro electric development in the Snare river drainage basin, by the crown, for the supply of power to the Yellowknife district where a demand for mining purposes already existed.
On February 15, 1946, an order in council, P.C. 507, was passed upon the recommendation of the Minister of Mines and Resources concurred in by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply under the authority of the Dominion Water Power Act, R.S.C., 1927, chapter 210, approving the construction in the name of His Majesty of the Snare river power development. The order also authorized the making of arrangements for the construction of a transmission line from the development to the Giant Yellowknife gold mines property, where an immediate market for power already existed.
Subsequently the deputy minister of justice expressed the opinion that, while the Dominion Water Power Act appeared to contemplate that such projects would be constructed on behalf of the crown, the act did not in express terms authorize such construction. In other words, his opinion was that the act did not provide the necessary authority for the order in council.
The development was proceeded with under authority of the wording of a vote approved by parliament for the project in the supplementary estimates for 1946-47, vote 775; and the wording of a vote approved by parliament for the project in the main estimates for 194748, vote 165. Similar authority is asked in the woiding of the vote submitted to parliament in the main estimates for 1948-49, vote 210. It was felt, however, that in view of the opinion of the deputy minister of justice the Dominion Water Power Act should be amended to remove all doubt as to the power of the governor in council to authorize the construction of power developments on behalf of the crown, if such construction were considered desirable.
Section 12 of the Dominion Water Power Act sets forth the various matters with which the governor in council may deal and the purpose of the bill is to insert after paragraph (o) of the original act a new provision:
(p) for the construction, maintenance and operation by the minister of any undertaking upon lands of the dominion; and"
The amendments provided by paragraphs (o) and (q) are of a minor nature only and do not in any way change the sense of paragraphs (o) and (p) of the original act which they replace.
This bill, which has been prepared by the deputy minister of justice, on enactment will provide authority for the construction of power developments on lands of the dominion on behalf of the crown.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. 209 (from the senate) to amend the National Parks Act.

National Parks Act
Pie said: Mr. Speaker. I should like to make a brief statement of further explanation in connection with this bill. There is little I can add to the explanation printed in the bill. However I would emphasize that the chief purpose of the bill is to consolidate the descriptions of the national parks of Canada, because this is very desirable from an administration viewpoint and for the convenience of those who desire the information. These changes were not included in the 1947 amendment of the National Parks Act, since the department was then completing arrangements with New Brunswick for a national park in that province and it was desired that the list of parks be complete.
The National Parks Act of 1930 cancelled three parks and confirmed the remainder as they then existed, with the exception of five, for which detailed descriptions were provided in the act.
All parks established prior to 1930 were set aside by order in council under the old Forest Reserves and Parks Act. There have been many changes in these parks since the first ones were established in 1911. Since the passing of the National Parks Act in 1930, three parks have been cancelled by legislation, namely, Wawaskey, Buffalo and Nemiskam.
A few changes have been made in the boundaries of some of the other parks. The Cape Breton Highlands national park and Prince Edward Island national park were established under provisions of the Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island National Parks Act of 1936 as amended. Some changes were made later in the boundaries of these parks.
The New Brunswick national park was established pursuant to the provisions of the National Parks Act of 1937, which made special provision for the establishment of this park.
It is considered that there will be few further changes, if any, in the present boundaries, and it is very desirable in the administration of these areas to have a complete description of each park duly authorized by statute. No doubt many hon. members have noticed that during the past year orders in council on a great many subjects have been consolidated and brought up to date. This has involved a great deal of labour, but it is hoped that the consolidation, now available as a result of this work, will be of great assistance and save much research.
The same idea is carried out in the bill now before the house. In other words, it will only be necessary to refer to the National Parks
Act as now amended to get a complete list of the parks.
The second section brings the practice for gazetting regulations under the National Parks Act in line with prevailing practice. Section 3 sets up the new schedule. Section 4 provides for the repeal of the special acts no longer necessary as a result of this consolidation.

Mr. Speaker,
I wanted to say just a few words with reference to national parks. I think it is a splendid idea to determine definitely the boundaries of these national parks. I am also pleased that we are to have a national park in New Brunswick. I believe the idea was first mooted in 1936, but inspections had been made even prior to that. The people of our province were disappointed that a park was not established at the same time as the parks in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. I think all the sites should have been chosen at the same time, because New Brunswick has lost considerable tourist revenue in the years from 1936 to 1948. Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia had no difficulty in choosing their park sites and the parks were developed shortly after the sites had been chosen.
Anyone who has visited the Cape Breton national park knows they have one of the finest parks in Canada. The national park in Prince Edward Island is small, but it is beautiful and is attracting a great many tourists from the United States and other parts of Canada.
Four or five sites in New Brunswick were inspected. There is a feeling, which I think is justified, in certain sections of the province that the best site was not chosen. I also understand that the site chosen was not the one recommended to the department. I realize that the minister who is now doing the work of this department is new to the department, but if he will go back in the records I think he will find that the present site was the second choice, not the first.
I do not want to condemn this site even though it was the second choice. It is in the county of Albert and the park takes in part of the bay of Fundy and some fine hills and lakes. The site which was the first choice was on the Saint John river. I should like to say to hon. members who have not visited that river that we consider that historically and geographically it is one of the finest rivers, not only in Canada but in the world. I am not so sure about the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), but I do know that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), who has lived on the Saint John, will bear out that statement. It has been called the Rhine of America.
